is_anopheles.evidence: Study tests Anopheles arabiensis (and laboratory colony An. gambiae s.s.) in laboratory bioassays and experimental hut trials in Tanzania (e.g. Page 2, 'Three different mosquito strains were evaluated in bioassays: 1. An. gambiae sensu stricto Kisumu strain... 2. An. arabiensis...').

reports_target_markers.evidence: No insecticide resistance target markers were genotyped. The authors only cite prior work regarding resistance mechanisms: 'Previous studies have shown the An. arabiensis population in this area to be pyrethroid-resistant, due to elevated mixed function oxidases and esterases rather than kdr mechanisms [21]' (Page 3).

reports_extractable_genotype_data.evidence: No genotype or allele frequency or count data are reported.

african_field_population.evidence: Field An. arabiensis adults entering experimental huts were collected in Pasua village, Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, and F1 An. arabiensis from Lower Moshi, Tanzania were used in bioassays (Page 2).

is_primary_study.evidence: This is a primary research paper evaluating indoor ATSB stations in experimental huts.

sub_country_location.evidence: Pasua village, Kilimanjaro, Tanzania (3°22'46S and 30°20'47E) and Lower Moshi, Tanzania (Page 2).

temporal_resolution_within_3y.evidence: The experimental hut trial ran between July 31 and August 19, 2012 (Page 3).

duplicate_risk.evidence: Standard experimental hut trial performed in 2012 without overlap with genomic consortia.

supplement.evidence: No supplementary files are referenced for molecular marker data.

assessment.summary: This study evaluated the efficacy of indoor attractive toxic sugar bait (ATSB) stations in laboratory cage bioassays and experimental huts in Pasua village, Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, against pyrethroid-resistant Anopheles arabiensis and Culex quinquefasciatus. No insecticide resistance target markers were genotyped.
